newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina to send labor reforms to Congress.
newsitem.headline: Argentina to send labor reforms to Congress.

text.p: Argentine President Carlos Menem said Tuesday he would send a labor reform agreement to Congress for approval.

Although he had failed to gain total business approval of an agreement reached earlier with the unions, Menem said at a news conference that the proposed reforms were tough enough to reduce Argentina's high unemployment rate.
"Maybe many people haven't realized yet, but these are the most profound reforms to labor legislation in 50 years," he said.
Menem was speaking after a final meeting with business and union representatives, after trying to get them to agree on reforms all year.

The powerful Group of Eight (G-8) business lobby produced its own document, calling for small companies to be able to negotiate wages directly with unions, and for private health funds to be able to compete with union funds.
The Peronist government desperately needs good news on unemployment, currently at 17.3 percent, before October's mid-term Congressional elections.

The International Monetary Fund recommended labor reforms as a way of reducing employment costs and Menem tried to push a tough reform package through by decree. Blocked by courts and hostile unions, he tried three-way talks and when they proved fruitless, he made a deal with unions.
Late last month, Menem went behind the backs of business leaders to sign a blueprint Act of Agreement with unions, which is a watered-down reform package.

The G-8 lobby blasted it as "useless" because it maintains union control over wage talks and drops plans to replace costly redundancy payouts with unemployment insurance. It also drops plans to force union-controlled healthcare schemes to compete with private firms in an open market.
